Unless otherwise specifically stated, the contents of this Handbook will be considered as standard policy by staff and students. The University of Lusaka was officially opened by Hon. Dr John N. T.

text: 1 1. 0 HISTORICAL BACKGROUND The University of Lusaka (UNILUS) is a modern university established under the University ACT. No. 11 of 1999 which has since been repealed and replaced by Act. No. 4 of 2013. The University of Lusaka takes pride in offering quality education. It is driven by its motto, Passion for Quality Education: Our Driving Force. At inception in 2007, the institution operated under the title, ‘Institute for Corporate Training and Applied Research’ (ICTAR). In January 2008, the institution was registered as a university. In the same year, the University of Lusaka introduced its Bachelor’s Degree programmes in partnership with the Copperbelt University; and in 2009 began offering its own programmes. The University of Lusaka was officially opened by Hon. Dr John N. T. Phiri, Minister of Education, Science, Vocational Training and Early Education, on Thursday 18th October, 2012. Following this auspicious beginning, the University now offers a wide range of programmes at Bachelors, Masters and Doctoral levels. Since inception, University of Lusaka has been working in collaboration with other universities, and notable among them are, the Copperbelt University, University of Zambia and University of KwaZulu Natal. University of Lusaka programmes combine the enduring value of a classroom education with skills and experiences of lecturers most of whom hail from industry; who ensure that students are engaged and equipped for successful careers and fulfilling lives. The University of Lusaka is one of Zambia’s first private universities established in 2007.

text: UNIVERSITY OF LUSAKA HANDBOOK 2 1.2 Mission Statement UNILUS mission is to promote equitable lifelong learning and socio- economic transformation of communities through interactive training and research in higher education and practical, community based problem solving initiatives. 1.3 Core Values The University has eight (8) core values in its contribution to the provision of education. These are: 1.3.1 Academic Freedom Academic freedom is the most fundamental value underpinning all our scholarly activity which is defined as freedom to conduct research, teach, speak and publish subject to the norms and standards of scholarly inquiry without interference or penalty, wherever the search for truth and understanding may lead. 1.3.2 Excellence The University of Lusaka challenges itself to come up with exemplary rather than satisfactory outcomes through innovation and creativity. 1.3.3 Quality and Achievement The University believes that it should provide a wide range of high-quality educational and scholarly opportunities that stimulate activity and recognise achievement by students, faculty, and staff. 1.3.4 Diversity The University believes that a university community connects the perspectives and backgrounds of diverse social and academic groups of people. 1.3.5 Collaboration The University contributes to the advancement of society by working as an engaged partner of business and industry, government bodies, accredited agencies and the community it serves.

text: A Senate shall consist of: (a) The Vice-Chancellor; (b) The Deputy Vice-Chancellor; (c) The Registrar; (d) The Deans of schools within the University; (e) Not more than fourteen professors and associate professors who are not members of the Senate by virtue of other provisions of this paragraph; and which number shall include at least one professor or associate professor from each school elected by the academic staff in accordance with such election procedures as the Senate may decide; (f) The Librarian; (g) The Directors of the centres, institutes, bureau or other similar bodies of the university; (h) The Dean of Students; (i) Not more than fourteen members of the non-professorial academic staff of the university from each academic unit, elected by the academic staff in accordance with such election procedures as the academic staff may determine; (j) Two students of the University who shall be elected by the students of the University in accordance with such election procedure as the University students’ union may determine; and (k) Not more than four persons appointed by the Vice- Chancellor who are resident in the Republic, are not employed as academic, administrative or other staff of the University and are capable of contributing to the academic development and life of the University.

text: UNIVERSITY OF LUSAKA HANDBOOK 7 3. 3 University Advisory Council The University Advisory Council is an independent committee established to provide guidance on management and decision making to the Board of Directors on the overall management and strategic direction of the university. The Council will also advise on submissions made by the other sub-committees. The terms of reference for the Council are set by the Board of Directors. The Council is composed of the following members appointed by the Board of Directors: (a) Chairperson; (b) Vice Chairperson; (c) Secretary; and (d) Council members. The Council meets twice a year and on an as-needed basis. Council members are kept abreast of University events through emails and other forms of communication. The Council consists of a broad cross-section of members from local and international business community. Members of the Council will normally serve a three- year term of office. The Chairperson of the Board is appointed by the Board of Directors; and when appointed, will serve for three years. 3. 4 Senate Sub-Committees In addition to the above specified committees, the University has constituted the following committees to ensure efficiency and effectiveness in the different areas of academia: (a) Curriculum Review Committee; (b) Calendar and Timetable Review Committee; (c) Student Admissions and Regulations Committee; (d) Academic Disciplinary Committee; (e) Strategic Review Committee; (f) Examination Committee; and (g) Research, Scholarship, Grants and Awards Committee; and (h) Exemptions Committee 3.

text: UNIVERSITY OF LUSAKA HANDBOOK 8 Functions The functions of the Committee are to: (a) advise on strategies and direction of the university, particularly in terms of issues such as corporate- orientated research, corporate engagement in general and executive education in particular; external image projection, identity and market positioning of the university; (b) assist in the establishment and development of the university’s position within various networks of practitioners locally, nationally and internationally; (c) advise on fund raising activities, including identifying opportunities especially those which are most relevant to the focus areas of the university; (d) act as a sounding board for new ideas and developments in the university; (e) assist the Executive Team to build and deliver cases for institutional change where these are required; and (f) provide appropriate and constructive challenges to the assumptions and operating routines of the university. Schedule of meetings and Mode of Communication The Committee meets twice a year and on an as-needed basis. The Committee members are kept abreast of university events through electronic media and other forms of communication. Composition The Committee consists of members drawn from a broad cross- section of local and the international business community, and should be diverse in terms of gender, sector and public and private ownership. The Chairperson of the Committee is appointed by the members of the Committee and serves for three years.

text: UNIVERSITY OF LUSAKA HANDBOOK 62 ECF 470 Environmental Economics 10. 3. 4. 9 Bachelor of Science in Economics and Finance The Bachelor of Science in Economics and Finance programme has a rare combination of courses in economics and finance. The programme has been designed to provide the economic reasoning, quantitative skills and institutional knowledge required by economists to solve practical problems. The degree offers the students an opportunity to combine in- depth studies in economics and finance. It provides students with the analytical tools from the fields of Mathematics, Statistics, Economics and Econometrics together with the institutional knowledge required to work as economists and financial analysts. The programme is grounded on Quantitative, Economics and Finance subjects. The Degree programme has optional units in economics and finance. More generally, the Degree is designed to develop good analytical skills which should be useful in the context of further studies or work. This programme will provide graduates with employment opportunities in the public and private sector, marketing research firms, management consulting firms, banks, securities and brokerage, and computer and data processing companies. The graduates will have opportunities to work at all levels of local and central government as well as non-profit and international organisations such as the World Bank (WB), Africa Development Bank (ADB) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

text: UNIVERSITY OF LUSAKA HANDBOOK 64 10.3.4.10 Bachelor of Science in Insurance and Pension Management This is a highly specialised course in business management that concentrates on the intricacies of the Insurance and Pension Management Sector. It prepares individuals to manage risk in organisational settings and provide insurance and risk-aversion services to businesses, individuals and other organisations. It also prepares graduates to plan and manage pension funds and social security schemes for wealth-creation since the industry is endowed with huge funds. As Zambia embraces market economics and foreign direct investments, the onus is on the entrepreneurs to manage risk and pensions of their employees. This course is suited for both specialisations. The graduates taking the course will be able to manage risk undertaken by an insurance company or pension fund. Therefore, graduates will be able to undertake actuarial positions and/or pension fund management activities. They will also be able to undertake analytical work in these fields. text: UNIVERSITY OF LUSAKA HANDBOOK 66 BIP 470 Real Estate Investment and Financial Analysis BIP 480 Asset Liability Management BIP 490 Real Estate Finance ***Electives are only offered subject to availability of minimum number of students and resources 10. 3. 4. 11 Bachelor Of Science In Actuarial Science Actuarial Science stands at the intersection of risk and money. It is a branch of science that uses Mathematics, Statistics, Economics and Financial knowledge to model and manage future uncertainty in financial, pension and insurance industries. Particularly, insurance firms, pension and benefit firms, financial institutions and other similar organizations require the services of actuaries in pricing products, and assess the risk of certain events occurring and to formulate policies that minimize the cost of that risk. Using their broad knowledge of mathematics, statistics, economics, finance, and business, actuaries help design insurance policies, pension plans, and other financial strategies in a manner which will help ensure that the plans are maintained on a sound financial basis. The main objective of the Bachelor of Science in Actuarial Science is to prepare students for a career as an actuarial scientist concerned with the construction of models and solutions for insurance, pension, financial, business and societal problems involving uncertain future events. The graduates of actuarial science are expected to find employment in insurance firms, pension and employee benefits firms, banks, consulting firms and brokerage firms.

text: UNIVERSITY OF LUSAKA HANDBOOK 103 MSP 720 Warehousing and Storage Management MSP 730 Marketing GBS 700 Research Methodology Stage 4 GBS 800 Dissertation 10. 7. 12 Master of Business Administration (MBA) in Healthcare Management The Master of Business Administration (MBA) in Healthcare Management is a postgraduate degree granted to students who complete a course of study in the knowledge and competencies required for careers in today’s modern healthcare administration. The MBA in Healthcare Management qualifies students for senior administrative and management positions in hospitals, health care organisations, public health administration, private clinics and other organisations that are concerned with the availability and quality of health services. The objectives of the MBA in Healthcare Management are : (a) to provide management education to medical professionals and others working in the field of health sector both in public and private; (b) to equip executives or managers concerned with health care administration with up-to-date knowledge about management and develop relevant skills and attitudes; and (c) to prepare such executives and managers to apply modern management techniques in managing both public and private health care services in Zambia. The MBA in Healthcare Management is intended for students who have studied medicine, nursing, dentistry, life science, microbiology, pharmacy, biotechnology, physiotherapy, veterinary science, paramedics, and related medical professions or fields.

UNIVERSITY OF LUSAKA HANDBOOK 108 Stage Four MEM 800 Applied Environmental Project and Dissertation 10.7.16 Master of Arts in Development Studies With a view of revolutionising application of development theories to accentuate developmental change in developing countries, the programme follows the experiential training format of applied theory on development. The programme aims at developing participants who will be grounded in theory and practice of social-economic and management sciences. The programme draws on experiences and lessons learnt from both developed and developing nations in other regions of the world. The programme is interdisciplinary in nature, focusing on development management, poverty reduction and human development. Stage One MDS 511 Advanced Development Thinking MDS 512 Agriculture and Rural Development MDS 513 Development Policy MDS 720 Gender and Development MDS 721 Development Management Stage Two GBEPM 520 Project Planning and Management GBEPM 740 Monitoring and Evaluation GBS 751 Entrepreneurship and Innovation MDS 618 Urban and Regional Planning GBS 700 Research Methodology Stage Three MDS 719 Environment and sustainable Development

text: UNIVERSITY OF LUSAKA HANDBOOK 109 Stage Four GBS 800 Research ***** Publication of Article in Recognised Journal 10.7.17 Master of Public Health (MPH) The programmes strategic goal is to develop health practitioners who will be fully equipped in both social and scientific approaches to promote the health of humankind through evidence based practice and interventions that prevent and control disease, injury and disability in a fast changing world. The programme, specifically is designed to ultimately: (a) equip students with public health knowledge; (b) identify potential risk factors and causes of ill health in populations; (c) develop strategies for health promotion to prevent and control ill health; (d) utilise a wide variety of approaches and skills to maintain health; and (e) disseminate public health services among the population. Stage 1 MPH 511 Global and Population health metrics MPH 521 Biostatistics MPH 531 Epidemiology MPH 541 Health Promotion and behavioural Sciences MPH 551 Introduction to Health policy and Systems Development MPH 561 Public Health Research A Research Methods I: Proposal Development and Designs B Statistical Computing (Access, Epidata, SPSS, and Nvivo skills) Stage 2 MPH 612 Public Health Informatics A Research methods II: Observational Designs B Statistical Analysis for Managers ( SPSS and Nvivo skills)

text: UNIVERSITY OF LUSAKA HANDBOOK 112 EXMBA 702: Innovation And Creativity EXMBA 801: Entrepreneur Development and Entreprise Ownership EXMBA 802: Financing EXMBA 803: Strategic Management EXMBA 900: Research 10. 7. 19 Master of Laws (LLM/MPhil) - Environmental Law The Master of Laws (LLM)/ Master of Philosophy (MPhil) in Environmental Law taught programme is aimed at offering candidates a unique opportunity to pursue personal intellectual development and career development in the field of environmental law. The LLM/MPhil in Environmental Law programme has been designed to train experts required in the field of environment in order to help address some of the major challenges posed by the degradation of the environment; and related issues at local, regional and international level. The LLM/MPhil in Environmental Law is open to lawyers and to non-lawyers who have degrees in other disciplines and working or intending to work in the environmental related fields. It provides candidates with opportunities to meet and learn from others involved in environment- related disciplines. The LLM/MPhil in Environmental Law programme is to be completed within twenty-four months. The programme is divided into three semesters. The first two semesters constitute the taught components whereas the last semester requires students to complete a master’s thesis.

text: UNIVERSITY OF LUSAKA HANDBOOK 125 Academic integrity is the moral code or ethical policy of academia. This includes values such as avoidance of cheating or plagiarism, fabrication and facilitation of academic misconduct; maintenance of academic standards; honesty and rigour in research and publishing. The set of core values underwrites the very mission of the University itself; integrity, honesty, hard work, and the determination to translate personal and professional principles into behaviour. As members of an academic community, we are entitled to a wide degree of freedom in the pursuit of scholarly interests. With that freedom, however, comes the responsibility to uphold the high ethical standards of academic conduct. It is a reflection of the students’ experience at University of Lusaka (UNILUS), and is a measure of the very worth of their degree. For students, this ethic lies at the heart of the value of their degree. If they or others around them are not living up to a high standard of academic integrity, the worth of the education they are receiving (and the degree they will receive) is compromised. A high standard of academic integrity will ultimately lead to greater heights of academic rigour and freedom among students, a better reputation for University of Lusaka (UNILUS), and more positive patterns of interaction with the student population. We can generate a long-lasting academic focus among the faculty population that migrates to UNILUS and the student population that passes through UNILUS.

text: The principles of academic integrity also represent an informal contract between faculty and students. Instead of pitting faculty against students, both share a common standard of behaviour and set of values critical to the continued success of the UNILUS. Both populations play an important role and have a responsibility in creating and constantly re-creating the strength and excellence defining UNILUS. For this purpose: (a) The University is committed to assuring ethical behaviour by all its members, and all members of the University community are expected to share in this commitment of ethical behaviour. Academic dishonesty is an offence against the University. A student who has committed an act of academic dishonesty has failed to meet a basic requirement of satisfactory academic performance. Thus, academic dishonesty is relevant to the evaluation of the student’s level of performance, and is also a basis for disciplinary action by the Registrar’s office.

text: UNIVERSITY OF LUSAKA HANDBOOK 126 (b) All members of the University community will maintain an environment in which each member is given equal opportunities to achieve academic success; and each member’s academic achievements are assessed fairly and objectively. (c) All members of the University will take active roles in the promotion and maintenance of academic integrity. These roles include, but are not limited to the following: (i) knowing and abiding by the academic regulations of the University; (ii) beginning each semester, the lecturer must inform the class of the policy regarding academic dishonesty; (iii) taking safeguards to deter the opportunistic violation of the academic regulations of the University; (iv) reporting any suspected acts of academic dishonesty to the appropriate party; and (v) ensuring that other members of the University are diligent in their responsibilities to the maintenance of academic integrity. (d) Students should report any suspected acts of academic dishonesty to the lecturer as soon as possible. The lecturer will then determine whether to submit a report as described in section 6 below: (i) the student’s report to the lecturer must include any information or evidence that can assist the lecturer in determining whether to pursue the alleged incident; (ii) the student’s report should include a description of the circumstances leading to the suspicions of academic dishonesty.

text: UNIVERSITY OF LUSAKA HANDBOOK 127 and (v) denial of access to resources (e. g. , reserved library material, laboratory material, art work, computer software) intended to be available to others. (f) Lecturers must notify students of their intention to report a suspected incident of academic misconduct within ten calendar days of detecting the incident. Lecturers must report, using Option A or Option B, the circumstances and academic assessment impact of any suspected acts of academic dishonesty to the Registrar’s office as soon as possible after notifying the student, but in no case longer than fourteen calendar days after notifying the student. The Registrar’s office will copy the report to the course department chair, the student’s divisional dean and the divisional dean of the course, and contact the student. Option A - Discussion Agreement Lecturers have the option to discuss the specific allegation with the student. If the lecturer and student agree on a sanction (e. g. , reduction in course grade, failing course grade, assignment of additional work), no disciplinary action will be taken by the Registrar’s office as a result of this specific act alone. If, however, this specific act represents the student’s second or greater instance of academic dishonesty, the Registrar’s office may choose disciplinary sanctions (e. g. , suspension, dismissal). The Lecturer must indicate on the form if no agreement was reached with the student. In all cases, the form, and relevant materials must be forwarded to the Registrar’s office for evaluation.

Regardless of the option used, lecturers may award a failing grade on the assignment, a failing grade in the course, or may otherwise adjust the assignment or course grade as deemed appropriate. text: UNIVERSITY OF LUSAKA HANDBOOK 128 Registrar’s office. (g) Grades are to be assigned based on the individual efforts of each student. No credit will be given for any work that does not represent the individual efforts of a particular student or his or her contribution to a collaborative effort. Lecturers are solely responsible for assessing academic performance, and the Registrar is solely responsible for the application of disciplinary measures. The Registrar will determine whether any punitive actions should be taken in response to an act of academic dishonesty, and the Registrar will determine the nature of any such actions in accordance with the rules and regulations of the University: (i) disciplinary proceedings may result in a hearing before a committee; (ii) any person connected to the events surrounding a suspected act of academic dishonesty (e.g., lecturer, teaching assistant, and classmate) is required to cooperate with the Registrar’s investigation; and (iii) disciplinary outcomes may include no action, a warning, probation, suspension, permanent expulsion from the University, and withholding of transcripts, diplomas and degrees. We are each called to take pride in our own ideas and to respect the work of others. Be original and thoughtful. It’s your degree!

text: Page 1 of 5 DEPARTMENT OF OPEN AND DISTANCE LEARNING GUIDE TO DISTANCE LEARNING REGISTRATION Distance students, like their full time and part time counterparts, are required to register for their courses and exams every semester. Upon registration ensure that the university calendar is collected or downloaded from the university website. The calendar has the dates for all university academic activities including dates and the deadlines for the two assignments, residential classes and examinations. ONLINE REGISTRATION The University has recently introduced online registration where you do not need to travel to the campus in Lusaka in order to register. All you have to do is to follow the following steps FIRST YEARS AND NEW STUDENTS: STEP ONE: Access the Unilus Website (www. unilus. ac. zm) and click on “Online Registration Tab”. A page will pop up showing the instructions for registration for new and returning students. STEP TWO: Click on "New student registration" STEP THREE: Enter your student number as it appears on your acceptance letter, and key it into the appropriate field either postgraduate or undergraduate, and click “OK’. Your Quotation will appear with all bank details on it. STEP FOUR: Print your quotation and then proceed to pay your school fees as indicated on you quotation, when making payments make sure you give your student number to the cashier. (e. g. BBA123456) STEP FIVE: After 48 hours from the time of payment Repeat steps 1 to 3, and click on a link “Click To register” just below Total fees on your quotation.

Content:
As a distance learning student you are required to read the material made available to you before you come for residential classes. Ensure that you complete filling in your personal details in your portal, especially your contact details. You are required to attend a two week residential classes session where you have full contact with your lecturers and immediately after the residential classes session ends you are required to write examinations in your registered courses. You will be notified well in advance as to the dates of the residential classes’ session. Before this you are free to consult your

text: Page 3 of 5 lecturers on your challenges in your study material by phone and by e-mail (with e-mail being more recommended). If you are in employment ensure that you have adequate leave days to attend both the residential classes and the examination – a total of 20 leave days. NOTE: It has been observed that distance learning students are very fond of removing furniture from classrooms for personal study. Please DO NOT remove desks and chairs from the classrooms during residential classes because you disturb the learning process. Classrooms may be used as study rooms if there are no classes taking place. No students should disturb the learning process on the pretext of studying. Distance residential classes are normally from 08 – 17 Hours and as such classrooms can be used as study rooms after classes. The habit of moving desks and chairs from classroom should be desisted from. PLEASE SERIOUSLLY TAKE NOTE OF THIS. ACCESSING MATERIAL AND ASSIGNMENTS. Reading material for all the courses and the assignments are uploaded by the lecturers and directly accessible by all registered students. To access these login into your student portal with your credentials. Once the student portal opens click on the “Materials” or the “Assignments “command tabs under the STUDENT MENU. For Materials you find a drop down list and choose the course whose material you are looking for. You then click on the “Search” command tab and the material will appear. For assignments you click on the “Assignments” command tab and the assignments for the courses you are registered in should appear.

text: Industry-Ready Graduates: 1,480 New Leaders Emerge from UNILUS “Passion for Quality Education: Our Driving Force” “LEAD with Vision and Purpose: Graduating with the Power of Self Resilience. ” This was the theme at the 17th graduation ceremony held by the University of Lusaka (UNILUS) on 24 and 25 April 2025 at its Silverest Campus in Chongwe District. The theme perfectly resonates with the high education standards of the ultra-modern private university, which prides itself on producing industry- ready graduates. This has been achieved through establishing strong linkages with industry and interaction with different stakeholders. The ceremony was officiated by UNILUS Vice Chancellor Pinalo Chifwanakeni. It was graced with the presence of various stakeholders, including vice chancellors of other universities and their deputies, registrars of other universities, professors and lecturers, sponsors, and UNILUS staff, among others. Zambia National Public Health Institute Director Mr. General Roma Chilengi and Chief Justice Mumba Malila were the guests of honour. The graduands, clad in their colourful gowns, were the main stars of the show. The University of Lusaka boasts five schools with various programmes under them, namely: School of Postgraduate Studies, School of Business and Economics and Management, School of Medicine and Health Sciences, School of Technology and Social Sciences, and the School of Law. Those who graduated were from various disciplines. Graduates celebrating during the their 17th graduation ceremony at Silverest Campus in Chongwe District.

text: UNILUS Sign MoU with Kumamoto University The University of Lusaka (UNILUS) has signed two Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with Kumamoto University (KUMADAI), a world-renowned institution in Japan. One MoU focuses on academic exchanges, while the other emphasizes student exchange programs. The event was witnessed by the Chief Representative of the JICA Zambia Office, Mr. Jotaro TATEYAMA, who represented the Vice-Chancellor of Kumamoto University, Dr. Hisao OGAWA who was accompanied by the JICA Project Formulation Advisor Ms. Megumi SUDA . Also in attendance were the UNILUS Vice-Chancellor, Prof. Pinalo Chifwanakeni, and other members of staff. Prof. Chifwanakeni stated that the two MoUs marks the beginning of a strong partnership between the two Universities and serve as a bridge connecting their academic visions. He noted that the collaboration will create valuable opportunities for both staff and students. The MoUs encompass several key pillars, including equipping students with advanced skills to drive innovation and entrepreneurship, providing continuous professional development for faculty, enabling joint research initiatives and academic publications in impactful fields, and enhancing community engagement through digital transformation initiatives, among others. The UNILUS Vice-Chancellor further revealed that the partnership with Kumamoto University is already underway, with some students set to travel to Japan in August for a one- year exchange program in the fields of Computer Science and Information Technology at no tuition cost.

text: “Passion for Quality Education: Our Driving Force” Government Urges Universities to Conduct Policy-Influencing Research at SARUA Conference Government has challenged universities in the country and the Southern African region to engage in impactful research that drives policy change and transforms communities. This call was made during the official opening of the Southern African Regional Universities Association (SARUA) Conference held under the theme: “Innovating Higher Education for Sustainable Development Across the SADC: Innovation for Impact. ” Speaking during the official opening of the conference Ministry of Education Permanent Secretary for Technical Services Dr. Kelvin Mambwe said there was need for research that was relevant and capable of changing lives. “The public must be able to see how research is transforming their lives,” he said. Dr. Mambwe welcomed regional delegates and commended SARUA for choosing Zambia, particularly the University of Lusaka, as the host venue. He said the hosting of the conference at a higher learning institution, instead of a hotel, was a symbolic step in promoting academic engagement. Dr Mambwe said Zambia’s investment in higher education, citing infrastructure development, digital transformation, and increased research capacity as key milestones. The conference, co-hosted by the University of Lusaka and the University of Zambia, brought together university leaders, researchers, from across the region.

text: “Passion for Quality Education: Our Driving Force” UNILUS Host EXMBA Students From Latvia Fourteen Executive MBA (EXMBA) students from RIGA Business School at the Technical University of Latvia have visited the University of Lusaka (UNILUS) in Zambia for a study module focused on sustainable business models and wealth creation, with a specific emphasis on Africa. An Executive MBA is a specialized master’s degree in business administration designed for experienced professionals in leadership or management roles who seek to advance their skills and careers. Upon arrival at Lusaka’s Kenneth Kaunda International Airport, the team was warmly received by Prof. Mlenga Jere, Deputy Vice Chancellor – Student Experience and Alumni Affairs, along with other UNILUS staff members. In his official welcome, UNILUS Vice Chancellor Professor Pinalo Chifwanakeni expressed his appreciation for the collaboration and emphasized the significance of the visit. He told the students that their trip would provide valuable insights into the vast business opportunities available in Zambia and across the African continent. Professor Chifwanakeni noted that Africa is richly gifted with natural resources and holds great potential in key sectors such as human capital, wildlife, tourism, and manufacturing.

text: Eva Kangwa, praised the students for their dedication to promoting a healthy environment, noting that this is not the first clean-up initiative undertaken by the University. text: “Passion for Quality Education: Our Driving Force” UNILUS, ZNS Sign a Five-Year MOU to Enhance Educational Opportunities The University of Lusaka (UNILUS) has signed a five-year Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Zambia National Service (ZNS) to expand educational opportunities for military personnel and their families. Under the agreement, ZNS officers, soldiers, civilian employees, and their children will receive a 15% tuition waiver for undergraduate and postgraduate studies at UNILUS, while ZNS will offer UNILUS students hands-on industrial training and practical exposure across various sectors. Speaking at the signing ceremony, UNILUS Vice-Chancellor, Professor Pinalo Chifwanakeni, expressed enthusiasm about the partnership, emphasizing its broader impact beyond academics to social and economic development. Professor Chifwanakeni further stressed the integration of research into training programs, stating that the collaboration would drive academic excellence, foster innovation, and contribute to Zambia’s national development through strategic research and training initiatives. Meanwhile, ZNS Deputy Commander and Chief of Staff, Major General Reuben Mwewa, described the partnership as a transformative step towards enhancing professional growth and operational efficiency within ZNS. He noted that, in return, ZNS would provide UNILUS students with practical exposure and industrial training in fields such as agriculture, engineering, logistics, private enterprise, and security studies.

text: “Passion for Quality Education: Our Driving Force” Dentsu Zambia & UNILUS Launch’s a Talent Incubator for Graduates Dentsu Zambia has officially launched the Dentsu Zambia Talent Incubator, a fresh and forward thinking partnership with the University of Lusaka (UNILUS) aimed at helping fresh graduates gain real world experience in media, marketing, and advertising. The initiative is designed to close the gap between classroom learning and the fast paced demands of today’s job market. Through mentorship, on job training, and direct exposure to global brands, graduates will have the chance to build the practical skills they need to succeed. With Zambia’s digital and creative industries on the rise, there’s growing demand for professionals who can navigate both local and international markets. The Talent Incubator offers just that an opportunity for young people to learn the modern trends in a real world setting while gaining insights into global industry standards. “This program is about more than just getting experience,” said Chishimba Musonda, Managing Director of Dentsu Zambia. “It’s about helping young Zambians shape their careers, learn from global leaders, and compete with confidence on the world stage. We’re proud to be investing in the country’s future. ” The incubator also reflects Dentsu’s broader commitment to Zambia’s development by nurturing home grown talent. The company hopes that this partnership with the University of Lusaka will inspire innovation and drive a long term growth within the country’s media and marketing sectors.

Speaking during the signing ceremony, UNILUS Vice Chancellor Professor Pinalo Chifwanakeni emphasized the importance of the collaboration in equipping students with practical skills in one of today’s most dynamic and in- demand fields digital marketing. “This partnership will empower our students with the hands-on experience they need to thrive in the digital economy,” Prof. Chifwanakeni said. “The true value of education lies in its ability to prepare learners to solve real world problems, engage with industry tools, and adapt to a rapidly evolving digital landscape.” He further highlighted that the collaboration would also foster research, innovation, and knowledge exchange key pillars in the university’s commitment to academic and professional excellence. Yellow Ray Digital Co-Founder and Creative Director, Adele Makayi, welcomed the partnership, noting its significance in advancing digital skills in Zambia. “This MoU signals the growing importance of digital competencies in today’s economy and reinforces our shared commitment to empowering Zambian professionals with practical, future oriented training,” she said. Makayi also revealed that Yellow Ray Digital has so far facilitated 13 cohorts

of its training program, benefiting 256 passionate and ambitious students. “Currently, we’re guiding a dynamic group of 19 learners through the latest cohort. We continue to be inspired by the creativity, curiosity, and resilience they bring to the classroom,” she added. UNILUS Vice Chancellor, Prof. Chifwanakeni, and Yellow Ray Digital Co-Founder and Creative Director, Adele Makayi, shake hands after signing the MoU. By Frank Mshanga

text: “Passion for Quality Education: Our Driving Force” UNILUS Business School Hosts Inaugural Career Fair Over 700 students attended the first-ever Career Fair at the School of Business, Economics, and Management, held in the auditorium at UNILUS Silverest Campus. The event was themed “Navigating the Modern Job Market: Insights from Industry Leaders. ”. The Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director of Standard Chartered Bank, Mr. Sonny Zulu, shared invaluable career insights and practical advice, drawing from his own experiences. Sonny emphasised that career success is not solely about academic excellence but also about making wise lifestyle choices, selecting the right networks, and being intentional about personal decisions. “Who are you? What is your purpose? ” he asked the students, adding that once individuals understand their identity and purpose, everything begins to fall into place. Mr. Zulu further encouraged students to embrace a world full of possibilities, stating that “the world is changing faster than ever imagined, and you are the key. The skills you develop, the knowledge you acquire, and the passion you nurture today will drive the next wave of innovation. Do not just adapt to the future—define it. ” CEO of Yenda, Krishma Nayee, a Zambian impact-driven entrepreneur passionate about breaking barriers to employment and financial freedom, delivered a presentation on navigating the modern job market using the internet. She provided insights on finding online job opportunities and leveraging digital tools for career advancement.

text: “Passion for Quality Education: Our Driving Force” Rekindling the Dying Embers Lately, I have been feeling rather ‘off ‘owing to my personal inner battles and questioning of the essence of life. Pondering on the realities of life, I have embraced a new conviction that every human being has a fire’ or ‘spark’ within that requires time and again to be rekindled. If this process is ignored, one tends to lose interest and passion to achieve their dreams. In fact you begin to question your relevance. This article is for one who has forgotten their worth and importance of their existence. It is for one who has quit on their pursuit as they question whether life is worth the living. For students this question may be influenced by many factors such as financial, academic, relational, family and general survival struggles. One life’s lesson is that the moment you begin to perceive life to be meaningless it means you expose your vulnerability to any form of destruction. When this occurs, it is time to REKINDLE that which is ‘dying’. To ‘rekindle’ would entail to light up, to fan into flames, so that the dying embers, or dying coal would light again. The reality of life is that with the passage of time, one tends to be overtaken by various life’s spears and experiences that deflates one’s passion in pursuing their dream and who they wished to be upon graduation. This can be translated into forgotten positive habits or life’s rituals that proved to give you energy to fight on.

text: For a student, it could be those positive habits that enhance your focus on your studies and your greatness that awaits to be exuded within your circles. It is the forgotten discipline to journal your feelings and emotions so that you remain in touch with reality. It could further be rituals of working out to enhance your mental health, reading some inspirational articles, fellowship with others, touching base with your spiritual growth among others. Remember, if the dying embers are never revisited, the seeds of greatness deposited in you are suffocated and never to germinate. ‘Rekindling the dying embers’ also suggest bringing to life that which brings a smile and sense of fulfillment and purpose in your life. It is the sharpening of your influence to people around you but more so your resilience to life’s challenging moments. Is it a talent or skill that has been halted and yet it screams within wanting to be given chance? Is it the business idea that got started but aborted along the way yet the passion still exists? Is it your relationship with your God that has gotten cold over the years and you no longer feel His existence nor presence? Is it your love and passion for your work that has been quenched over time due to various reasons? A reminder to you is that it is not too late to shine again. Your fire can burn brighter and hot again. You can still shine brighter within your circles and touch lives in ways untold. Your dreams can begin to receive and ounce of hope and expectation to soar high.

text: The University of Lusaka (hereinafter referred to as “UNILUS” or “the University”) was established as a centre of excellence dedicated to delivering academic and professional training enriched with value addition. The Student Code of Conduct and Disciplinary Procedures (hereinafter referred to as “the Code”) serves as a guiding framework for student behaviour within the University community. Accordingly, all students who choose to pursue their studies at the University are bound by the Code and are expected to conduct themselves with civility and propriety at all times, whether on or off campus. 2. 0 SCOPE The Code of Conduct applies to all students of the University. It applies to: a) Activities in which they engage in as students of the University; or b) Services or facilities they enjoy by being students of the University; or c) Their presence in the vicinity of, or their access to, any premises owned, leased or managed by the University; or d) Any activity not covered by (a), (b) or (c) above, which is considered to adversely affect the safety, interests or reputation of the University, its students, employees or authorised representatives. 3. 0 DEFINITIONS Academic Integrity: commitment to, and demonstration of honest and moral behaviour in an academic setting. Appeal: earnest request for aid, support, mercy and sympathy. Assault causing bodily harm: shall have the meaning as defined in the Penal Code Cap 87 of the Laws of Zambia. Breach: infraction or violation of law, trust, faith or promise.

Students are prohibited from failing to exit or from impeding the orderly evacuation of any facility, property, or building when a fire alarm or other emergency notification has been sounded. Furthermore, no student shall intentionally set fires in any University facility, on any person, or on campus without proper authority. It is equally prohibited to intentionally initiate or cause any false report, warning, or threat of fire, explosion, terrorism, or other emergencies, including knowingly reporting a false emergency. 7. 1.

text: A student shall not engage in examination malpractice which shall include but is not limited to the following: (a) A student shall not introduce, or attempt to introduce, into any venue where an examination is being conducted or is about to be conducted, any book, note, mobile phone, electronic device, or other instrument capable of storing, sending, or receiving information, nor any article containing information, unless expressly authorised by the examiner, the Examinations Officer, or the Chief Invigilator. (b) The possession, use, or attempted use, during an examination of any book, note, mobile phone, or other electronic device or instrument capable of storing, sending or receiving information, or any other article containing information, the use of which is not authorised by the examiner or the examinations officer or Chief Invigilator.

(b) The possession, use, or attempted use, during an examination of any book, note, mobile phone, or other electronic device or instrument capable of storing, sending or receiving information, or any other article containing information, the use of which is not authorised by the examiner or the examinations officer or Chief Invigilator.

text: (c) The removal or attempted removal from an examination room of any examination book or writing paper supplied by the University to answer an examination; (d) The removal of any page from the Examination Answer Booklet, or tearing of any section or part of a question paper; (e) The communication or attempted communication of any information relating to an examination to any candidate while the examination is in progress; (f) The use of a false name or identification number in an examination; (g) The submission for examination as own work any written matter or project which has been copied, reproduced or extracted, in whole or in part, from the work of another, or which is substantially the same, in whole or in part, as the work of another; (h) Intentionally assisting another student to cheat; (i) The commission of any other fraudulent, deceitful or dishonest practice whereby any student, while being examined by the University, seeks to mislead or deceive the Examiner or the Examinations Officer or Chief Invigilator. (j) Writing or attempting to write an examination in a course that does not appear on the confirmation of registration slip and examination docket and the name of the student does not appear on the examination register. A reprimand serves as a disciplinary sanction and forms part of the student's disciplinary record. It may be considered in determining sanctions for any subsequent misconduct. 10. 3. 2 Suspension Suspension means the temporary withdrawal of a student's right to attend classes, participate in academic or extracurricular activities, access University facilities, reside in University accommodation, or enjoy any other privileges of student status for a specified period and subject to such conditions as the University may impose. A student who has been expelled shall cease to be a student of the University and may only be readmitted in exceptional circumstances and in accordance with the University's policies, if at all. A student who is expelled from the University is nonetheless responsible for all financial obligations which he or she has incurred to the University. 10. 3.

text: 4 Fines and Reparation Fine means a monetary penalty imposed on a student as a disciplinary sanction for misconduct. A fine shall be payable within the period prescribed by the University, and failure to pay the fine may result in additional disciplinary or administrative action in accordance with University policies. Reparation (Restitution) means an order requiring a student to repair, replace, restore, or compensate for any loss, damage, destruction, or injury caused by the student's misconduct. Reparation may include payment for damaged property, reimbursement of financial loss, restoration of University property, or any other appropriate form of compensation determined by the University. The University can impose fines or reparation either in their own right or in addition to other punishment meted out. (a) Any fine or reparation imposed shall be paid by the student or student organisation to the Accounts Office of the University following the order passed by the Student Disciplinary Committee.

A fundamental pillar of university research is the translation of research outputs into innovation, creating commercial products that drive progress and societal impact. This issue proudly highlights the establishment of the Centre for Research Innovation, Consultancy and Commercial Development (CRICCD), a strategic initiative aimed at bridging research excellence with industry application, fostering innovation, and enhancing commercial viability. text: Page : 3 In June 2025, the University of Lusaka appointed Professor Jason Mwanza as Research Coordinator, further strengthening the University’s research portfolio and expanding its reach into the Social Sciences. Professor Mwanza brings a wealth of experience in research, having served for several years as a Senior Lecturer at the University of Zambia. His extensive contributions to academia include a Hirsch index of 12 and over 47 publications listed on Google Scholar. Holding a PhD in Sociology, Professor Mwanza’s expertise will undoubtedly enhance the University’s research initiatives, fostering innovation and academic excellence across disciplines. AI conference on Research Regulation In June 2025, the University of Lusaka participated in a conference on research regulation hosted in Cape Town by Ethiexpert, the manager of the Rhinno Ethics Platform. This platform is dedicated to streamlining the ethical review process for research proposals conducted by Institutional Ethical Review Boards (IRBs). The University of Lusaka was among the first higher education institutions (HEIs) in Zambia to adopt the Rhinno Ethics Platform, beginning in April 2024. At the conference, the University was represented by Mrs. Musonda Mubanga Phiri, further demonstrating its commitment to advancing ethical research practices. A key outcome of this conference was the consensus on leveraging AI to accelerate ethical reviews conducted on this digital platform.

text: As part of its ongoing research activities, the UNILUS Research Ethics Committee (REC) reviews over 400 proposals each semester, highlighting the importance of efficient, AI-driven ethical review processes. Professor Jason Mwanza Appointed as Research Coordinator Telling the story of Research In May 2025, the University of Lusaka School of Medicine and Health Sciences launched its first-ever Research Club, driven by students’ desire to engage in scientific inquiry and innovation from an early stage in their academic journey. This initiative was inspired by the POHER annual international conference, held in November 2024 at the University of Lusaka Silver Rest Campus. The event attracted over 400 students from around the world, who presented research papers across various disciplines. The enthusiasm and knowledge exchanged at this gathering motivated students to establish a Research Club, fostering a culture of inquiry and scholarly collaboration. To mark the club’s official launch, Professor Kasonde Bowa, Deputy Vice Chancellor for Research, was invited as the guest speaker. He shared his remarkable journey in research, which began in his sixth year of medical training when his professor in Obstetrics and Gynecology mentored him in refining McDonald’s rule, replacing the traditional finger method with a measuring tape for enhanced accuracy. Professor Bowa’s dedication to research has earned him notable recognition, including the Researcher of the Year Award in 2023, presented by the Minister of Science and Technology.

text:
The University of Lusaka (UNILUS) is a modern, dynamic private institution established under the University Act No. 11 of 1999, later replaced by the Higher Education Act No. 4 of 2013 and The Higher Education (Amendment) Act No. 23 of 2021. Founded in 2007 as the Institute of Corporate Training and Research (ICTAR), the University initially focused on postgraduate education through a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Copperbelt University. Since then, UNILUS has evolved into a fully independent and reputable university offering a diverse portfolio of academic programmes at Bachelor’s, Master’s, and Doctoral levels. Today, the University offers more than 24 undergraduate programmes, 43 postgraduate programmes, several postgraduate diploma programs, over 16 doctoral degrees, and a range of professional short courses tailored to meet industry needs. UNILUS is a thriving multi-cultural institution with a diverse and growing student population. The University maintains strong academic partnerships with institutions across the country, Africa, Europe and thw world at large. It now operates three campuses in Lusaka, namely:

• Pioneer Campus – Off Alick Nkhata Road, Mass Media
• Law Campus – Off Leopards Hill Road, New Kasama
• Silverest Campus – Along the Great East Road in Chongwe

text: From an initial enrolment of only 71 students in 2007, the University now boasts over 16,800 students, With a distinguished faculty comprising experienced professionals and accomplished academics, UNILUS blends rigorous academic learning with practical, industry-driven skills. UNILUS boasts of modern learning facilities and is led by qualified local and international staff, who are dedicated to delivering quality education. The University offers full-time, part-time (evening classes) and distance learning modes, with two enrolment intakes each year (January and June). The University continues to grow from strength to strength, reaffirming its commitment to excellence in higher education and its role in shaping future leaders for Zambia, the region, and beyond.

text: A Tier One classified institution by the Higher Education Authority of Zambia recognized for it’s commitment to academic excellence, research and innovation , and industry relevant education. Recognised & Accredited – Fully accredited under Zambia’s Higher Education framework with qualifications recongnized locally and internationally. Career-Focused Education – Industry-informed programmes that emphasize employability, internships, mentorship, and practical skills. Modern & Relevant Curricula – Courses regularly updated to meet market demands in high-growth fields such as Law, Business, Health Sciences, ICT, and Cybersecurity. Flexible Study Options – Full-time, part-time (evening), distance learning Online learning, and block release modes, with two intakes per year. (I. e. January and June). Wide Range of Programmes – Undergraduate, postgraduate, and executive programmes across diverse disciplines. Qualified Faculty & Modern Facilities – Experienced local and international lecturers supported by modern classrooms, Lecture theatre, laboratories, and libraries. Strategic Location in Lusaka – Access to business, government, NGOs, and research institutions for real-world learning and networking. Practical & Community Engagement – Hands-on learning through real-world projects, legal aid clinics, outreach, and entrepreneurship initiatives. Multicultural & Supportive Environment – Diverse student body with accommodation, clubs, sports, mental health, and international student support.

School of Medicine and Health Sciences At the end of each semester, students can view their examination results and comments on the student portal. Each course will show a grade or comment explaining the outcome. Common Examination Comments

• NE (Not Examined): one did not sit for the exam or results were not entered.
• S (Satisfactory): one passed a non-graded course, such as a project.
• WP (Withdrawn with Permission): You were officially allowed not to sit the exam.
• Repeat Course: one must retake the failed course(s).
• Repeat Semester: one must repeat the entire semester.
• Repeat and Proceed: one carry the failed course(s) into the next semester.

The goal of the University of Lusaka is to respond to the needs of its stakeholders in order to become a major player in the provision of tertiary education. 1.0 HISTORICAL BACKGROUND

The University of Lusaka (UNILUS) is a modern university established under the University ACT. No. 11 of 1999 which has since been repealed and replaced by Act. No. 4 of 2013. The University of Lusaka takes pride in offering quality education. It is driven by its motto, Passion for Quality Education: Our Driving Force. At inception in 2007, the institution operated under the title, ‘Institute for Corporate Training and Applied Research’ (ICTAR). In January 2008, the institution was registered as a university. In the same year, the University of Lusaka introduced its Bachelor’s Degree programmes in partnership with the Copperbelt University; and in 2009 began offering its own programmes. The University of Lusaka was officially opened by Hon. Dr John N.T. Phiri, Minister of Education, Science, Vocational Training and Early Education, on Thursday 18th October, 2012. Following this auspicious beginning, the University now offers a wide range of programmes at Bachelors, Masters and Doctoral levels.

The University of Lusaka was officially opened by Hon. Dr John N.T. Phiri, Minister of Education, Science, Vocational Training and Early Education, on Thursday 18th October, 2012. Following this auspicious beginning, the University now offers a wide range of programmes at Bachelors, Masters and Doctoral levels.

Since inception, University of Lusaka has been working in collaboration with other universities, and notable among them are, the Copperbelt University, University of Zambia and University of KwaZulu Natal. University of Lusaka programmes combine the enduring value of a classroom education with skills and experiences of lecturers most of whom hail from industry; who ensure that students are engaged and equipped for successful careers and fulfilling lives.

text: A Senate shall consist of: (a) The Vice-Chancellor; (b) The Deputy Vice-Chancellor; (c) The Registrar; (d) The Deans of schools within the University; (e) Not more than fourteen professors and associate professors who are not members of the Senate by virtue of other provisions of this paragraph; and which number shall include at least one professor or associate professor from each school elected by the academic staff in accordance with such election procedures as the Senate may decide; (f) The Librarian; (g) The Directors of the centres, institutes, bureau or other similar bodies of the university; (h) The Dean of Students; (i) Not more than fourteen members of the non-professorial academic staff of the university from each academic unit, elected by the academic staff in accordance with such election procedures as the academic staff may determine; (j) Two students of the University who shall be elected by the students of the University in accordance with such election procedure as the University students’ union may determine; and (k) Not more than four persons appointed by the Vice- Chancellor who are resident in the Republic, are not employed as academic, administrative or other staff of the University and are capable of contributing to the academic development and life of the University.

The Bachelor of Laws degree offered by UNILUS has enjoyed popularity over the years as it offers a variety of courses some of which are not offered elsewhere in the country. 10. 1. 2 The Board of Studies

text: 41 body, was established to, inter alia, review, hear and make decisions related to student appeals; make recommendations on matters of policy arising from the Board discussions to the Senate; and serve as the final body of academic appeal in the School. The Board of Studies is composed of the following members: (a) the Dean of the School as Chairperson; (b) all faculty staff of the School; (c) representatives from the other Schools; (d) Distance Education Coordinator; (e) Librarian; (f) a representative of the Registrar; and (g) Dean of Students. 10. 1. 3 The Board of Examiners The Board of Examiners oversees all examinations and recommends to the Senate graduands for the award of degrees. The composition of the Board of Examiners is composed of the following members: (a) the Dean of the School as Law; (b) all faculty staff; (c) a representative from the other Schools; (d) representative of the Registrar; (e) the Librarian; and (f) student Counselor (g) Dean of Students. 10. 1. 4 School Programmes The UNILUS Bachelor of Laws (LLB) degree is a unique programme offered to law candidates in Zambia; and is designed to meet the ever growing legal challenges that a lawyer is likely to encounter in his career in Private Practice, Government and Statutory Bodies, Corporate or Business world, International Organisations as well as those who wish to study law in order to assist them pursue their personal interests.

ECF 470 Environmental Economics 10.3.4.9 Bachelor of Science in Economics and Finance The Bachelor of Science in Economics and Finance programme has a rare combination of courses in economics and finance. The programme has been designed to provide the economic reasoning, quantitative skills and institutional knowledge required by economists to solve practical problems. The degree offers the students an opportunity to combine in- depth studies in economics and finance. It provides students with the analytical tools from the fields of Mathematics, Statistics, Economics and Econometrics together with the institutional knowledge required to work as economists and financial analysts. The programme is grounded on Quantitative, Economics and Finance subjects. The Degree programme has optional units in economics and finance. More generally, the Degree is designed to develop good analytical skills which should be useful in the context of further studies or work. This programme will provide graduates with employment opportunities in the public and private sector, marketing research firms, management consulting firms, banks, securities and brokerage, and computer and data processing companies. The graduates will have opportunities to work at all levels of local and central government as well as non-profit and international organisations such as the World Bank (WB), Africa Development Bank (ADB) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF). The graduates will have opportunities to work at all levels of local and central government as well as non-profit and international organisations such as the World Bank (WB), Africa Development Bank (ADB) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF). text:

The programme aims to provide students with a basic, balanced and advanced background in principles, foundations; and scientific theories in the various fields of management. This will ensure that graduating students are capable of thinking, structuring, analysing and solving world problems. Environmental Law programme has been designed to train experts required in the field of environment in order to help address some of the major challenges posed by the degradation of the environment; and related issues at local, regional and international level. The LLM/MPhil in Environmental Law is open to lawyers and to non-lawyers who have degrees in other disciplines and working or intending to work in the environmental related fields. It provides candidates with opportunities to meet and learn from others involved in environment- related disciplines. The LLM/MPhil in Environmental Law programme is to be completed within twenty-four months. The programme is divided into three semesters. The first two semesters constitute the taught components whereas the last semester requires students to complete a master’s thesis. text: 125 Academic integrity is the moral code or ethical policy of academia. This includes values such as avoidance of cheating or plagiarism, fabrication and facilitation of academic misconduct; maintenance of academic standards; honesty and rigour in research and publishing. The set of core values underwrites the very mission of the University itself; integrity, honesty, hard work, and the determination to translate personal and professional principles into behaviour. As members of an academic community, we are entitled to a wide degree of freedom in the pursuit of scholarly interests. With that freedom, however, comes the responsibility to uphold the high ethical standards of academic conduct. It is a reflection of the students’ experience at University of Lusaka (UNILUS), and is a measure of the very worth of their degree. For students, this ethic lies at the heart of the value of their degree. If they or others around them are not living up to a high standard of academic integrity, the worth of the education they are receiving (and the degree they will receive) is compromised. A high standard of academic integrity will ultimately lead to greater heights of academic rigour and freedom among students, a better reputation for University of Lusaka (UNILUS), and more positive patterns of interaction with the student population. We can generate a long-lasting academic focus among the faculty population that migrates to UNILUS and the student population that passes through UNILUS.

text: The principles of academic integrity also represent an informal contract between faculty and students. Instead of pitting faculty against students, both share a common standard of behaviour and set of values critical to the continued success of the UNILUS. Both populations play an important role and have a responsibility in creating and constantly re-creating the strength and excellence defining UNILUS. For this purpose: (a) The University is committed to assuring ethical behaviour by all its members, and all members of the University community are expected to share in this commitment of ethical behaviour. Academic dishonesty is an offence against the University. A student who has committed an act of academic dishonesty has failed to meet a basic requirement of satisfactory academic performance. Thus, academic dishonesty is relevant to the evaluation of the student’s level of performance, and is also a basis for disciplinary action by the Registrar’s office.

126 (b) All members of the University community will maintain an environment in which each member is given equal opportunities to achieve academic success; and each member’s academic achievements are assessed fairly and objectively. (c) All members of the University will take active roles in the promotion and maintenance of academic integrity. These roles include, but are not limited to the following: (i) knowing and abiding by the academic regulations of the University; (ii) beginning each semester, the lecturer must inform the class of the policy regarding academic dishonesty; (iii) taking safeguards to deter the opportunistic violation of the academic regulations of the University; (iv) reporting any suspected acts of academic dishonesty to the appropriate party; and (v) ensuring that other members of the University are diligent in their responsibilities to the maintenance of academic integrity.

(d) Students should report any suspected acts of academic dishonesty to the lecturer as soon as possible. The lecturer will then determine whether to submit a report as described in section 6 below: (i) the student’s report to the lecturer must include any information or evidence that can assist the lecturer in determining whether to pursue the alleged incident; (ii) the student’s report should include a description of the circumstances leading to the suspicions of academic dishonesty. (e) Academic dishonesty refers to any act that is intended to produce an academic assessment that is not commensurate with an individual’s performance, or any act that is intended to unfairly assist or hinder an individual’s academic efforts. Such acts include, but are not limited to the following: (i) allowing the work of one person to be academically assessed as the work of another; (ii) allowing academic credit to be assigned to work that was not performed;

Lecturers must report, using Option A or Option B, the circumstances and academic assessment impact of any suspected acts of academic dishonesty to the Registrar’s office as soon as possible after notifying the student, but in no case longer than fourteen calendar days after notifying the student. The Registrar’s office will copy the report to the course department chair, the student’s divisional dean and the divisional dean of the course, and contact the student. Option A - Discussion Agreement Lecturers have the option to discuss the specific allegation with the student. If the lecturer and student agree on a sanction (e. g. , reduction in course grade, failing course grade, assignment of additional work), no disciplinary action will be taken by the Registrar’s office as a result of this specific act alone. If, however, this specific act represents the student’s second or greater instance of academic dishonesty, the Registrar’s office may choose disciplinary sanctions (e. g. , suspension, dismissal). The Lecturer must indicate on the form if no agreement was reached with the student. In all cases, the form, and relevant materials must be forwarded to the Registrar’s office for evaluation. Option B - Academic Integrity Violation Report If the lecturer chooses not to complete the discussion agreement, he or she must nonetheless notify the student, complete the Academic Integrity Violation Report, attach relevant materials, and forward this information to the Registrar’s office.

Stuck? Quick fixes

Forgot your password?＋

Use the "Forgot password" link on the Google sign-in screen, or reach out to UNILUS IT support to reset it for you — don't keep guessing, too many wrong tries can lock the account.

Account locked out?＋

This usually happens after several failed sign-in attempts. Contact the IT help desk and they'll unlock it and confirm your details.

Not sure of the exact email format?＋

Every student address ends in @stud.unilus.ac.zm. An example is 2026321789@stud.unilus.ac.zm or bit21276734@stud.unilus.ac.zm , If you're unsure of the exact spelling, check your admission letter or ask the registry/IT desk to confirm it before you try logging in.

text:
Leopards Hill Campus Help desk assisted

How do I connect to campus Wi-Fi? Go to your device's Wi-Fi settings, select the UNILUS network, and sign in with your student email credentials. At Silverest and Pioneer campuses, connect to eduroam instead using your full institutional email and password. Gmail isn't loading — what can I try? Clear your browser cache, try a different browser, or check your network connection. If the issue persists, contact the Help Desk. Moodle file upload or quiz isn't working Confirm your file is under the size limit and that your internet connection is stable before uploading. Refresh and retry if a quiz fails to load. How do I change or reset my password? Use the self-service password reset portal. If you're locked out entirely, contact the IT Help Desk for manual verification.

text:
Follow the steps below to complete your school fees payment through Airtel Mobile Money.

01

Step 1 — Initiate

Dial the Airtel Money USSD Code

On your Airtel line, open your phone dialer and enter the code below, then press Call / Send.

*115#

02

Step 2 — Navigate

Select "Make Payment"

A menu will appear on your screen. Choose the Make Payment option from the list.

1. Send Money

2. Airtel Money Plus

3. Buy Airtime & Bundles

4. Make Payment ← Select

5. Withdraw Cash

03

Step 3 — Category

Choose "School Fees"

From the payment categories, select option 7. School Fees.

1. Utilities

2. Insurance

3. Government

4. DSTV / TV

5. Merchants

6. Hospital Bills

7. School Fees ← Select

04

Step 4 — Biller

Select "Zanaco Bill Master"

You will be prompted to choose a biller. Search or scroll to find and select Zanaco Bill Master.

1. Copperbelt University

2. UNZA

3. Zanaco Bill Master (UNILUS) ←

4. Mulungushi University

text: PRICED – UNILUS The PRICED Centre supports research, innovation, consultancy, and development. It provides a framework for publications, applied research, customised training, and encourages postgraduate students and post-doctoral researchers to engage in impactful activities aligned with the university’s mission. Applied Research The Centre fosters academic and collaborative research through proposal training, approach testing, funding support, and research assistance. It promotes knowledge sharing and international collaboration to support Zambia’s economic and social growth. Publication PRICED offers a supportive framework for publishing and disseminating research. It encourages academic staff and students to produce peer-reviewed publications that enhance UNILUS’s scholarly reputation. Consultancy The Centre empowers academic staff to contribute to societal development by offering consultancy services aligned with their expertise. This enhances the University’s community engagement and professional impact. Customised Training PRICED develops and delivers short-term, need-based training programs tailored for organizations, NGOs, individuals, and private companies—supporting capacity development across sectors.

Section: B. Study Permit Application Information
Content:
The University of Lusaka continues to advocate for international students, including on matters related to immigration. Please take note of the following guidelines regarding the study permit process:

text:
- You may apply for your study permit as soon as you receive your acceptance letter.
- Any student enrolled for six (6) months or longer must apply for a study permit, including visiting or exchange students.
- SADC students: Apply once registered and physically in Zambia.
- Non-SADC students: Apply for a visa in your home country before travelling; once in Zambia, apply for a study permit.

text: 1. How do I log in? Use your student portal login credentials to log in to the E-Learning platform. 1. I can’t log in to the eLearning platform but can access the student portal. Make sure you are registered for the semester and if so reset your pasword from your student portal account Reset from here. 2. What is the difference between the Moodle App and the eLearning website? The Moodle App is a mobile version for access on-the-go. The website offers full functionality. 3. What link do I use to connect the Moodle App? Use the link: https://elearning. unilus. ac. zm when adding your site in the app. 4. How do I find my courses on the eLearning Platform? Once logged in, navigate to your dashboard. All enrolled courses are listed under "My Courses. " 5. How do I attempt a quiz? Use the link: https://host. unilus. app/ to log into the online assessments platform, select my courses choose the desired course the quiz should be one of the first notices. 6. How do I submit an assignment? Log into the eLearning search for the desired course and click on it, the assignment should be one fo the first options. 7. How do I get my ID processed as a new student? Please send an email to id@unilus. ac. zm with a passport-sized photograph attached, clearly indicating the campus from which you wish to collect your ID card.. 8. How do I submit an assignment through the plagarism checker? Once the assignment is posted on the eLearning platform, wait a few minutes and the percentage of your document will appear. 9. How do I contact my lecturers or course coordinators?

text:
Passion for Quality Education: Our Driving Force

The University of Lusaka (UNILUS) is guided by its unwavering commitment to delivering quality education. Through this dedication, the University continues to shape futures, empower students, and contribute meaningfully to national and global development.

Established in 2007 as the Institute for Corporate Training and Applied Research (ICTAR), the institution was registered as a university in January 2008 and introduced its first Bachelor’s Degree programmes in the same year.

The University was officially opened on 18 October 2012 by John N.T. Phiri, then Minister of Education, Science, Vocational Training and Early Education.

text:
The University was officially opened on 18 October 2012 by John N.T. Phiri, then Minister of Education, Science, Vocational Training and Early Education.

Since its inception, UNILUS has grown into one of Zambia’s leading private universities, offering a diverse portfolio of undergraduate and postgraduate programmes. The University has positioned itself as a Centre of Excellence in education, training, research, and consultancy services.

The University’s programmes are designed to respond to evolving industry demands and societal needs within a rapidly changing technological environment. By aligning its curriculum with both public and private sector expectations, UNILUS ensures that its graduates are well-prepared to contribute to economic development and innovation.

Est. 2007 · Lusaka, Zambia

The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is a four-year programme that goes beyond basic programming to provide a solid grounding in computing concepts, theories and emerging technologies. It focuses on both the theoretical and practical aspects of software and computational systems, with core strengths in software theory, design, development and application.

Students are prepared to design algorithmically complex software and solve real-world computational problems. Key areas of study include mathematical foundations, algorithms and problem-solving, artificial intelligence, computer systems and networks, security, databases, human–computer interaction, graphics and vision, numerical analysis, programming languages, software engineering, bioinformatics and the theory of computing.
